quote: Wahrscheinlich giebt es keine[?] solche [-V-] Verzweigungselemente ausser bei der durch die lineare Integralgl. vermittelten Beziehung.
english: Probably there are no such branch elements except in the relation mediated by the linear integral equation.
topic: Hilbert discusses, by analogy with power series expansion and Riemann surfaces, when the linear variation of one solution curve depends uniquely and invertibly on that of another, identifying 'branch elements' as those satisfying the Lagrange differential equation (vanishing of the first variation), and proposes studying curves without inflection points.

triage.modern_statement: Here is one plausible reading; the note is too brief to be sure. Take a family of extremals, meaning solutions of the Euler–Lagrange equation. Map the data of one curve (for example its boundary or initial data) to the data of another. When is this map locally one-to-one with a one-to-one linearization? It fails to be invertible at 'branch elements', where the linearized problem has a nontrivial solution. That linearized problem is the vanishing first variation, i.e. the Jacobi (accessory) equation, which Hilbert recasts as a linear integral equation. On this reading the conjecture says: branching can only happen where the associated linear (integral) equation has a nontrivial solution, i.e. at an eigenvalue or degenerate point. In modern terms, bifurcation points of a nonlinear (integral or variational) equation are confined to points where the linearized operator is not invertible. This follows from the implicit function theorem and is made precise by the Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction.
triage.answered_by: The closest documented match is Erhard Schmidt, Hilbert's student: 'Zur Theorie der linearen und nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen, III. Teil: Über die Auflösung der nichtlinearen Integralgleichungen und die Verzweigung ihrer Lösungen', Math. Ann. 65 (1908), 370–399. It builds on A. M. Lyapunov's 1906–1914 work on equilibrium figures of rotating fluids. This later became the Lyapunov–Schmidt method of bifurcation theory, developed further by Vainberg–Trenogin (1962) and others. I found no source that refers to this specific diary note.

evidence.claim: Schmidt (1908, Math. Ann. 65:370–399) dealt with solving nonlinear integral equations and the branching (Verzweigung) of their solutions. This work is a primary source for the Lyapunov–Schmidt method.

A history of nonlinear integral equations traces bifurcation theory from Lyapunov and Poincaré through Hilbert's school (E. Schmidt), Lalescu and Bratu. It cites Schmidt's 1908 paper on the branching of solutions.

triage.why: The note is a short heuristic remark in a calculus-of-variations setting and is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Its most natural modern reading is that branching or bifurcation of solutions happens only where the linearized (Jacobi or linear integral) equation is degenerate. That principle was made rigorous within Hilbert's own circle by E. Schmidt in 1908, building on Lyapunov, and is now standard (Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction, the implicit function theorem). Bifurcation theory is still an active research field, but this particular claim is settled. Confidence is low because the wording ('such branch elements', 'the relation mediated by the linear integral equation') is ambiguous. I could not tie the note directly to a later publication, so the link to Schmidt is my own inference from the subject matter and timing.
